pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Tipperary, founded 1180 by Donal Mor O'Brien; it held a relic of the true cross and was the chief pilgrimage of medieval Ireland)
etymology: From the relic that gave the house its name, Latin Sancta Crux; Irish Mainistir na Croiche Naofa, the monastery of the holy cross.
biblical_def: Holycross on the Suir was founded in 1180 by Donal Mor O'Brien, king of Thomond, and took its name and its fortune from a relic said to be a fragment of the cross of Christ. Pilgrims came from across Ireland; the fifteenth-century rebuilding, with its sedilia and its ribbed vaults, was paid for out of their offerings. The church was re-roofed and reopened for parish worship in 1975 and is one of the few medieval Irish abbeys still in use. The entry turns on a distinction the New Testament makes and a relic cult erases. Paul never speaks of the wood; he speaks of the message. “For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God” (1Co 1:18) locates the power in the proclamation, and his one boast is of the event, not the timber: “But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world” (Gal 6:14). The cross he glories in has already crucified him to the world, which no fragment in a reliquary can do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cross as a gibbet consisting of two pieces of timber placed across each other, and figuratively the sufferings of Christ; and relic as the remains of the body of a saint.
webster_full: CROSS, n. A gibbet consisting of two pieces of timber placed across each other, either in form of a T or of an X. The instrument of punishment on which our Savior suffered. Hence, the sufferings of Christ.
RELIC, n. That which remains; that which is left after the loss or decay of the rest. The body of a deceased person, or some part of it; the remains of a saint.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable.
PREACHING, n. The act of pronouncing a sermon; a public discourse on a religious subject.
GLORY, v.i. To exult with joy; to rejoice. To boast; to be proud of.
scriptures: For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.
Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
corruption_summary: The chief pilgrimage of medieval Ireland, built on a fragment of wood, and the apostle who gloried only in the preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the relocation of power from the word preached to an object possessed. A relic can be owned, guarded, charged for and lost; a message cannot. The economics follow the theology exactly, which is why the great rebuilding at Holycross is datable to the height of the pilgrim traffic. Paul stakes everything on the opposite: “But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness” (1Co 1:23) — a method with no artefact in it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the apostolic narrowing of subject matter: “For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1Co 2:2). That is not anti-intellectualism; it is the refusal of every supplement, whether a relic, a technique or a spectacle. The abbey standing re-roofed on the Suir is a better witness as a place where the word is preached than it ever was as a shrine.
roots_summary: Latin crux, a cross; Greek stauros (G4716), a cross; Greek logos (G3056), word or message; Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim; Greek kauchaomai (G2744), to boast or glory.
roots_lines: Latin Sancta Crux — the holy cross, the abbey's name.
Greek stauros (G4716) — an upright stake, a cross; “save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal 6:14).
Greek logos (G3056) — word, message; “For the preaching of the cross” (1Co 1:18).
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, to preach; “But we preach Christ crucified” (1Co 1:23).
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to boast, to glory; “that I should glory” (Gal 6:14).
usage: “but unto us which are saved it is the power of God” (1Co 1:18) — the power is in the preaching.
“by whom the world is crucified unto me” (Gal 6:14) — what no fragment accomplishes.
“save Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1Co 2:2) — the whole subject.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Burren, County Clare, founded about 1195; its Latin name was Sancta Maria de Petra Fertili, of the fertile rock)
etymology: From the Irish territory of Corco Modhruadh, the people of Modhruadh, with the abbey's Latin style de Petra Fertili, of the fertile rock.
biblical_def: Corcomroe stands in the Burren of County Clare, a landscape of bare grey limestone pavement where soil gathers only in the grikes between the slabs. The monks who founded it about 1195 called it Sancta Maria de Petra Fertili — St Mary of the fertile rock — which is either a joke or a confession of faith, and the carved capitals of its chancel, with their opium poppies and lilies, suggest the second. The phrase is biblical. Moses sang that God “made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock” (Deu 32:13), and the Psalmist repeats the promise in the Lord's own voice: “with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee” (Psa 81:16). The rock in both places is not a metaphor for difficulty overcome by effort. It is the hardest possible ground named precisely so that the sweetness drawn from it can only be credited to God. The Burren is such ground, and the abbey's name says so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fertile as fruitful, rich, producing fruit in abundance; and flint as a very hard stone, a variety of quartz, used in striking fire with steel.
webster_full: FERTILE, a. Fruitful; rich; producing fruit in abundance; as fertile land or soil.
FLINT, n. A sub-species of quartz, of a yellowish or blackish gray; a very hard stone, used in striking fire with steel.
ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter, usually compounded of two or more simple minerals. In Scripture, defense; means of safety; protection; strength.
HONEY, n. A sweet vegetable juice collected by bees from the flowers of plants, and deposited in the cells of the comb.
BARREN, a. Not producing young, or offspring. Not producing plants; unfruitful; sterile.
scriptures: He made him ride on the high places of the earth, that he might eat the increase of the fields; and he made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock;
He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee.
Job 28:9
He putteth forth his hand upon the rock; he overturneth the mountains by the roots.
And they thirsted not when he led them through the deserts: he caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them: he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out.
corruption_summary: An abbey on bare limestone that called itself St Mary of the Fertile Rock, and the honey Scripture draws out of flint.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption near this entry is the self-congratulating reading of hardship — the monastic and modern conviction that austerity itself produces fruit, and that a hard place is therefore a holy one. The Burren produced nothing because it was hard. Isaiah keeps the agency where it belongs: “he caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them: he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out” (Isa 48:21). The rock did not yield; it was cleft.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is pleased to feed his people from places that cannot feed them, and that this is the point rather than an inconvenience. Job observes of the miner that “He putteth forth his hand upon the rock; he overturneth the mountains by the roots” (Job 28:9) and yet cannot find wisdom there. Men can quarry a rock. Only God gets honey out of one.
roots_summary: Irish Corco Modhruadh, the territory; Latin Petra Fertilis, fertile rock; Hebrew sela (H5553), a crag; Hebrew challamish (H2496), flint; Hebrew debash (H1706), honey.
roots_lines: Latin de Petra Fertili — of the fertile rock, the abbey's own style.
Hebrew sela (H5553) — a crag, a cliff; “to suck honey out of the rock” (Deu 32:13).
Hebrew challamish (H2496) — flint, hard stone; “and oil out of the flinty rock” (Deu 32:13).
Hebrew debash (H1706) — honey; “with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee” (Psa 81:16).
Hebrew baqa (H1234) — to cleave, to split open; “he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out” (Isa 48:21).
usage: “that he might eat the increase of the fields” (Deu 32:13) — said of a people in a wilderness.
“He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat” (Psa 81:16) — the promise withheld by unbelief.
“he caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them” (Isa 48:21) — the agency, named.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Galway, founded 1190 by Cathal Crovderg O'Conor; its chancel wall carries a painting of the Three Living and the Three Dead)
etymology: Irish Mainistir Chnoc Muaidhe, the monastery of the hill of Muaidh, with the Latin name Collis Victoriae, the hill of victory.
biblical_def: Abbeyknockmoy was founded in 1190 by Cathal Crovderg O'Conor, king of Connacht, who was buried there in a monk's habit in 1224. On the north wall of its chancel survives a rare medieval Irish wall painting: three crowned kings in their robes face three corpses, and the legend under them warns the living that they will one day be what the dead now are. It is the standard medieval memento mori, and its theology is almost entirely sound. Ecclesiastes recommends the same exercise and gives the reason: “It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart” (Ecc 7:2). David turns it into a prayer — “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am” (Psa 39:4) — and Hebrews supplies the clause the painting usually leaves off: “as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mortality as subjection to death, the necessity of dying; and corpse as the dead body of a human being.
webster_full: MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death, or the necessity of dying. Death; as the mortality of a man.
CORPSE, n. The dead body of a human being.
FRAIL, a. Weak; infirm; liable to fail and decay; subject to casualties; easily destroyed.
MOURNING, n. The act of sorrowing or expressing grief; lamentation; sorrow.
JUDGMENT, n. The act of judging; the act or process of the mind in comparing its ideas. The final trial of the human race.
scriptures: Ecc 7:2
It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart.
Psa 39:4
LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am.
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
corruption_summary: Three kings face three corpses on a Connacht wall, and the clause the picture usually leaves out.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the memento mori that stops at mortality. A painting which says only that the great will rot produces either despair or a shrug, and the late Middle Ages produced plenty of both. Hebrews refuses to let death be the last fact: “but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) is the half that makes the first half matter, and the very next verse puts Christ's one offering against it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the contemplation of death is prescribed as a means to wisdom, not to gloom: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12). The modern error runs the other way from the medieval one — a culture that hides its corpses has made the exercise impossible and has not thereby escaped the appointment.
roots_summary: Irish Cnoc Muaidhe, the hill of Muaidh; Latin Collis Victoriae, hill of victory; Hebrew ebel (H60), mourning; Hebrew chadel (H2310), frail or fleeting; Greek krisis (G2920), judgment.
roots_lines: Irish Cnoc Muaidhe — the hill of Muaidh, Latinised Collis Victoriae.
Hebrew ebel (H60) — mourning; “to go to the house of mourning” (Ecc 7:2).
Hebrew chadel (H2310) — fleeting, frail; “that I may know how frail I am” (Psa 39:4).
Greek apokeimai (G606) — to be laid up, appointed; “as it is appointed unto men once to die” (Heb 9:27).
Greek krisis (G2920) — judgment, decision; “but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27).
usage: “and the living will lay it to his heart” (Ecc 7:2) — the purpose of the painting.
“make me to know mine end” (Psa 39:4) — mortality turned into prayer.
“but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) — the clause the wall omits.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Meath, founded 1147; the second house of the order in Ireland, and a party to the quarrel over the body of Hugh de Lacy)
etymology: Irish Beigtheach, the small house, with the Latin name Beatitudo Dei, the blessedness of God.
biblical_def: Bective was founded in 1147 by Murchad O'Melaghlin, king of Meath, as a daughter of Mellifont and the second Cistercian house in Ireland; its abbot sat in the parliament of the Pale. Its strangest hour came after 1186, when Hugh de Lacy, lord of Meath, was killed by a workman at Durrow. His headless body was buried at Bective and his head at St Thomas's in Dublin, and the two houses then litigated for fifteen years over which should hold the whole man, the case going to Rome before the body was finally surrendered to Dublin in 1205. Scripture records one dispute over a body, and uses it to teach restraint: “Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee” (Jud 1:9). The archangel had the better case and the greater power and did not raise his voice. Two monasteries fighting fifteen years over a corpse had neither excuse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contend as to strive in opposition, to struggle, to dispute earnestly; and sepulture as burial, interment, the act of depositing the dead body of a human being in the grave.
webster_full: CONTEND, v.i. To strive in opposition; to struggle. To dispute earnestly; to strive in debate.
SEPULTURE, n. Burial; interment; the act of depositing the dead body of a human being in the grave.
RAILING, n. Reproachful or insolent language. Clamorous abuse.
LITIGATION, n. The act or process of carrying on a suit in a court of law or equity; a judicial contest.
REBUKE, v.t. To chide; to reprove; to reprehend for a fault; to check by reproof.
scriptures: Jud 1:9
Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.
Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
corruption_summary: Two abbeys that went to law for fifteen years over a dead man's body, and the archangel who did not raise his voice over another.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is litigation between churches, and Paul treats the fact of the suit as the defeat regardless of its outcome: “Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong?” (1Co 6:7). The question is rhetorical and the answer at Bective was that a body was worth money in offerings and burial fees. Fifteen years and an appeal to Rome over a corpse is what the apostle meant by a fault.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the manner as well as the substance: Michael “durst not bring against him a railing accusation” (Jud 1:9) when disputing with the devil himself. If that is the standard toward an enemy, the standard between two houses of the same order is not lower. Proverbs gives the mechanism: “A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger” (Pro 15:1).
roots_summary: Irish Beigtheach, the small house; Latin Beatitudo Dei; Greek diakrino (G1252), to dispute; Greek blasphemia (G988), railing; Greek hettema (G2275), a defeat or fault.
roots_lines: Irish Beigtheach — the little house; Latin Beatitudo Dei.
Greek diakrino (G1252) — to contend, to dispute; “when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses” (Jud 1:9).
Greek blasphemia (G988) — reviling, railing; “durst not bring against him a railing accusation” (Jud 1:9).
Greek hettema (G2275) — a loss, a fault, a defeat; “there is utterly a fault among you” (1Co 6:7).
Hebrew rak (H7390) — soft, tender; “A soft answer turneth away wrath” (Pro 15:1).
usage: “The Lord rebuke thee” (Jud 1:9) — the whole of the archangel's argument.
“Why do ye not rather take wrong?” (1Co 6:7) — the question put to both abbeys.
“live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) — so far as it lies in you.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Limerick, founded 1148 by Turlough O'Brien, reputedly in thanksgiving for a victory over the Norse of Limerick)
etymology: Irish Mainistir an Aonaigh, the monastery of the fair or assembly, with the Latin name Magium after the river Maigue.
biblical_def: Monasteranenagh was founded in 1148 by Turlough O'Brien, king of Thomond, a daughter of Mellifont, and tradition attaches the foundation to a battle won against the Norse of Limerick on the nearby hill. Its carved capitals are among the finest Romanesque work in Ireland. A monastery endowed as the price of a victory is the commonest kind of foundation there is, and the Psalter deals with the instinct behind it carefully. It does not forbid thanksgiving for a battle; it forbids the accounting that credits the winner. “For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them” (Psa 44:3). The clause at the end is the one that disqualifies every victory monument: it was favour, not merit, and “neither did their own arm save them” (Psa 44:3). A house built on that confession is a true thank-offering. A house built to commemorate the arm is a trophy with a chapel attached.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thanksgiving as the act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies; and trophy as a pile of arms taken from a vanquished enemy, raised on the field of battle.
webster_full: THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
TROPHY, n. Among the ancients, a pile of arms taken from a vanquished enemy, raised on the field of battle by the conquerors.
VICTORY, n. Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest.
FAVOR, n. Kind regard; kindness; countenance; propitious aspect; friendly disposition.
DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty.
scriptures: Psa 44:3

For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them.
Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake.
Then Samuel took a stone, and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us. Ebenezer: that is, The stone of help
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
corruption_summary: An abbey endowed out of a victory, and the psalm that refuses to credit the sword that won it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the battle monument in religious dress. A king who builds a monastery after a victory has done something better than building an arch, and has often done it for the same reason. The Psalter answers with a doxology that leaves the builder nothing: “Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake” (Psa 115:1). The doubling of the first clause is not rhetoric; it is how hard the thing is to say once.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Samuel's kind of memorial, which names the help rather than the helper: he “called the name of it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” (1Sa 7:12). A stone that says that is a thank-offering. The word hitherto is doing real work — it claims nothing about tomorrow's battle.
roots_summary: Irish Mainistir an Aonaigh, monastery of the assembly; Hebrew yeshuah (H3444), salvation; Hebrew ratson (H7522), favour; Hebrew zeroa (H2220), an arm; Hebrew eben ha-ezer, the stone of help.
roots_lines: Irish Mainistir an Aonaigh — the monastery of the fair or assembly.
Hebrew zeroa (H2220) — an arm, strength; “neither did their own arm save them” (Psa 44:3).
Hebrew ratson (H7522) — favour, goodwill; “because thou hadst a favour unto them” (Psa 44:3).
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight; “but unto thy name give glory” (Psa 115:1).
Hebrew azar (H5826) — to help; “Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” (1Sa 7:12).
usage: “but thy right hand, and thine arm” (Psa 44:3) — the only true account of a victory.
“Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us” (Psa 115:1) — said twice, because once is not enough.
“Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” (1Sa 7:12) — the inscription for a thank-offering.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Kerry, founded 1154; known in its own charters as de Kyrie Eleison, of Lord have mercy)
etymology: Irish Mainistir O dTorna, the monastery of the O'Torna; its Latin name was Abbatia de Kyrie Eleison, from the Greek Kyrie eleeson, Lord have mercy.
biblical_def: Abbeydorney in north Kerry was founded in 1154 as a daughter of Monasteranenagh, and its charters style it de Kyrie Eleison — the abbey of Lord-have-mercy. Nothing much is known of its history and almost nothing of it stands, which leaves the name doing all the work, and the name is one of the oldest prayers in the church. It comes into the liturgy from the Greek of the Gospels, where blind men and foreigners and a desperate father all use it, and it is the whole prayer of the publican: “And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner” (Luk 18:13). Christ's verdict on that prayer is the verdict on the doctrine of justification: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other” (Luk 18:14). David's version adds the ground on which mercy is asked, which is never the asker: “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness” (Psa 51:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mercy as that benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves; and supplication as humble and earnest prayer.
webster_full: MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves; the disposition that tempers justice.
SUPPLICATION, n. Entreaty; humble and earnest prayer in worship.
PUBLICAN, n. A collector of toll or tribute. Among the Romans, a farmer of the taxes and public revenues.
JUSTIFY, v.t. In theology, to pardon and clear from guilt; to absolve or acquit from guilt and merited punishment.
LOVINGKINDNESS, n. Tender regard; mercy; favor.
scriptures: And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
Psa 51:1

To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.
And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.
corruption_summary: An abbey whose Latin name was the prayer Kyrie eleison, and the publican who prayed it and went home justified.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the Kyrie worn smooth by repetition until it is a musical form rather than a plea. The prayer is the shortest and most complete in Scripture, and it loses everything the moment the one praying it stops meaning the last two words. The publican's posture is given in detail precisely because the detail is the prayer: he stood afar off, he would not lift his eyes, he smote his breast.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that mercy is asked on the ground of God's character and never on the asker's. “according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions” (Psa 51:1) offers no mitigating circumstance. The Canaanite woman prays the same prayer with no claim at all — “Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David” (Mat 15:22) — and is answered.
roots_summary: Greek Kyrie eleeson, Lord have mercy; Greek hilaskomai (G2433), to be propitious; Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; Hebrew chanan (H2603), to show favour; Hebrew chesed (H2617), lovingkindness.
roots_lines: Greek Kyrie eleeson — Lord, have mercy; the abbey's Latin style.
Greek hilaskomai (G2433) — to be propitiated, to be merciful; “God be merciful to me a sinner” (Luk 18:13).
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous; “this man went down to his house justified” (Luk 18:14).
Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to be gracious, to show favour; “Have mercy upon me, O God” (Psa 51:1).
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant love, lovingkindness; “according to thy lovingkindness” (Psa 51:1).
usage: “standing afar off” (Luk 18:13) — the posture is part of the prayer.
“justified rather than the other” (Luk 18:14) — the verdict on two prayers.
“Have mercy on me, O Lord” (Mat 15:22) — prayed by a woman with no claim.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey below the Rock of Cashel, County Tipperary; granted to the Cistercians in 1272 after the archbishop expelled its Benedictines)
etymology: Irish an Iubhair, of the yew, anglicised Hore; the Latin name was Sancta Trinitas de Rupe, the Holy Trinity of the Rock.
biblical_def: Hore Abbey stands in the fields directly below the Rock of Cashel. It had been a Benedictine house, and in 1272 Archbishop David MacCarvill expelled the Benedictines and gave the place to Cistercians from Mellifont, endowing it richly out of the lands of his own see. The reason recorded by the annalists is that the archbishop had dreamed the Benedictines meant to behead him. Whatever the dream was, it served a decision he had use for, and the town of Cashel lost revenues the archbishop had transferred. Jeremiah deals with the dream offered as warrant and does so with unusual sharpness. “I have heard what the prophets said, that prophesy lies in my name, saying, I have dreamed, I have dreamed” (Jer 23:25), and then the ruling that separates the two kinds of speech for good: “The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat?” (Jer 23:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dream as the thought or series of thoughts of a person in sleep; and pretext as pretense, false appearance, ostensible reason or motive assigned or assumed as a color or cover.
webster_full: DREAM, n. The thought or series of thoughts of a person in sleep. In Scripture, dreams were sometimes impressions on the minds of men in sleep, made by divine agency.
PRETEXT, n. Pretense; false appearance; ostensible reason or motive assigned or assumed as a color or cover for the real reason or motive.
CHAFF, n. The husk or dry calyx of corn and grasses. Refuse; worthless matter.
WHEAT, n. A plant of the genus Triticum, and its seed, from which is made the finest and whitest bread.
EXPEL, v.t. To drive out; to force out, by force or authority.
scriptures: I have heard what the prophets said, that prophesy lies in my name, saying, I have dreamed, I have dreamed.
The prophet that hath a dream, let him tell a dream; and he that hath my word, let him speak my word faithfully. What is the chaff to the wheat? saith the LORD.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
Deu 13:1
If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder,
corruption_summary: An archbishop who expelled one order and endowed another, and said he had dreamed it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the private revelation that arrives exactly when a man needs a warrant. Jeremiah does not accuse the dreamers of inventing the dreams; he accuses them of passing a dream off as the word, and the distinction is maintainable whatever the dreamer's sincerity. “they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16) describes a man who may be perfectly honest about what he saw and entirely wrong about where it came from.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the test Moses laid down, which is doctrinal rather than evidential: even a dreamer whose sign comes to pass is to be rejected if he turns the people after other gods, for “If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder” (Deu 13:1) is followed by the command to try the content. Impressions are not authority. “let him speak my word faithfully” (Jer 23:28) remains the whole commission of a preacher.
roots_summary: Irish an Iubhair, of the yew; Hebrew chalom (H2472), a dream; Hebrew mots (H4671), chaff; Hebrew bar (H1250), grain or wheat; Hebrew sheqer (H8267), falsehood.
roots_lines: Irish an Iubhair — of the yew tree; Latin Sancta Trinitas de Rupe.
Hebrew chalom (H2472) — a dream; “I have dreamed, I have dreamed” (Jer 23:25).
Hebrew mots (H4671) — chaff; “What is the chaff to the wheat?” (Jer 23:28).
Hebrew bar (H1250) — winnowed grain, wheat.
Hebrew chazon (H2377) — a vision; “they speak a vision of their own heart” (Jer 23:16).
usage: “that prophesy lies in my name” (Jer 23:25) — the charge, and it concerns attribution.
“let him tell a dream” (Jer 23:28) — permission, with a label attached.
“and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16) — the only question that matters.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Tipperary, founded 1182 as a daughter of Jerpoint; its carved screen wall includes a mermaid beside a crucifixion)
etymology: Irish Cill Chuile, the church of the corner or nook, with the Latin name Arvicampus, the field of ploughland.
biblical_def: Kilcooly was founded in 1182 by Donal Mor O'Brien as a daughter of Jerpoint, burnt in 1445 and rebuilt, and its chief curiosity is the carved stone screen between the south transept and the sacristy. On it, within a few feet of each other, are a crucifixion, a bishop, the arms of the Butlers, two fish, and a mermaid holding a mirror and a comb. The mermaid is a standing medieval emblem of vanity and seduction, and she is carved inside the church. The mixture is the entry. Paul will not allow it: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?” (2Co 6:14). The question he presses next is the one a carved mermaid in a chancel answers badly: “And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God” (2Co 6:16). The sculptor may have meant her as a warning; the setting makes her furniture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines yoke as a piece of timber hollowed so as to fit the neck of an ox, and a bond or tie; and communion as fellowship, intercourse between two persons or more.
webster_full: YOKE, n. A piece of timber, hollowed or made curving near each end, and fitted with bows for receiving the necks of oxen. A mark of servitude; slavery. A bond or tie.
COMMUNION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; interchange of transactions or offices.
SYNCRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance.
MERMAID, n. A marine animal, said to resemble a woman in the upper parts of the body, and a fish in the lower part.
SCREEN, n. Any thing that separates or cuts off inconvenience, injury or danger; shelter; protection.
scriptures: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?

And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
corruption_summary: A mermaid carved a few feet from a crucifixion, and the apostle who will not allow the mixture.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is syncretism by accumulation. Nobody decides to place a sea-siren beside a crucifixion; she arrives by stages, as ornament, as a moral emblem, and finally as part of the furniture, and by then nobody asks. Elijah's question on Carmel is the right one and it is addressed to people who thought they were still worshipping the LORD: “How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him” (1Ki 18:21).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the apostolic command to separate, which is not a command to withdraw from society but to refuse the yoke: “Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you” (2Co 6:17). The promise attached is the reason it is not mere negation.
roots_summary: Irish Cill Chuile, the church of the nook; Greek heterozugeo (G2086), to be unequally yoked; Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; Greek sugkatathesis (G4783), agreement; Hebrew pasach (H6452), to limp or halt.
roots_lines: Irish Cill Chuile — the church of the corner; Latin Arvicampus.
Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be yoked with one of a different kind; “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2Co 6:14).
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, participation; “what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness?” (2Co 6:14).
Greek sugkatathesis (G4783) — agreement, assent; “And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols?” (2Co 6:16).
Hebrew pasach (H6452) — to limp, to hop between; “How long halt ye between two opinions?” (1Ki 18:21).
usage: “what communion hath light with darkness?” (2Co 6:14) — asked of a chancel screen.
“for ye are the temple of the living God” (2Co 6:16) — the reason the mixture matters.
“if the LORD be God, follow him” (1Ki 18:21) — the question that ends accumulation.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Cork, founded 1170 as a daughter of Inislounaght; its Latin name was Castrum Dei, the castle of God)
etymology: Irish Mainistir Fhear Maighe, the monastery of the men of the plain, with the Latin style Castrum Dei, the castle of God.
biblical_def: Fermoy on the Blackwater was founded in 1170 as a daughter of Inislounaght and called in its charters Castrum Dei. The house itself is gone and the modern town covers it, so the name is again what remains, and it is a name the Bible uses constantly for God himself and never for a building. Nahum states it in the middle of a book of judgement, which is where it belongs: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him” (Nah 1:7). The second clause is the one that distinguishes the doctrine from superstition — the stronghold knows who is inside it. David says the same with the same restraint: “He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved” (Psa 62:2). The word greatly is doing honest work. A castle of God is not a promise of no shaking; it is a promise of no overthrow.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stronghold as a fastness, a fort or fortress, a place of security; and defense as that which opposes attack, a fortification, protection.
webster_full: STRONGHOLD, n. A fastness; a fort or fortress; a fortified place; a place of security.
DEFENSE, n. Any thing that opposes attack, violence, danger or injury; fortification; guard; protection; security.
FORTRESS, n. A fortified place; a fort; a castle; a strong hold; a place of defense or security.
TRUST, v.i. To be confident, as of something present or future; to have reliance or confidence.
TROUBLE, n. Disturbance of mind; agitation; commotion of spirits; perplexity; affliction; calamity.
scriptures: Nah 1:7
The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
Psa 62:2
He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
The way of the LORD is strength to the upright: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity.
corruption_summary: An abbey called the Castle of God that has entirely vanished, and the stronghold that is a person.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the transfer of the name to the structure. Once an institution is called the castle of God, its walls begin to carry a theological claim they cannot bear, and when they fall the claim seems to fall with them. Fermoy is gone and Nahum's sentence is unaffected, because the stronghold he names was never masonry and his book is about the fall of a famously impregnable city.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the same strength is a stronghold to one man and a destruction to another, which Proverbs states without softening: “The way of the LORD is strength to the upright: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity” (Pro 10:29). The security is not in the shelter but in whose it is, which is why “he knoweth them that trust in him” (Nah 1:7) is attached to the promise and not detachable from it.
roots_summary: Irish Fear Maighe, men of the plain; Latin Castrum Dei, castle of God; Hebrew maoz (H4581), a stronghold; Hebrew misgab (H4869), a high refuge; Hebrew sur (H6697), a rock.
roots_lines: Irish Mainistir Fhear Maighe — the monastery of the men of the plain.
Latin Castrum Dei — the castle of God, the abbey's charter name.
Hebrew maoz (H4581) — a fortified place, a stronghold; “a strong hold in the day of trouble” (Nah 1:7).
Hebrew misgab (H4869) — a high place of refuge, a defence; “he is my defence” (Psa 62:2).
Hebrew sur (H6697) — a rock, a cliff; “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psa 18:2).
usage: “and he knoweth them that trust in him” (Nah 1:7) — the stronghold knows who is inside.
“I shall not be greatly moved” (Psa 62:2) — honest about the shaking.
“but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity” (Pro 10:29) — the same strength, two ends.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in County Kilkenny founded 1204, and the town that grew around it; also called Duiske)
etymology: Irish Graig na Manach, the village of the monks; the abbey itself was Vallis Sancti Salvatoris and is known from the river Duiske.
biblical_def: Duiske Abbey was founded in 1204 by William Marshal as a daughter of Stanley in Wiltshire, and became the largest Cistercian church in Ireland. What makes the place unusual is its name: the town is called Graig na Manach, the village of the monks, because the settlement was and is defined by the house at its centre. The abbey church was never wholly abandoned; after centuries of partial ruin it was restored and remains the Catholic parish church of the town. A community so visible that the place is named after it stands under a text that is both promise and warning. “Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14) is not advice to be conspicuous; it is a statement of fact about what the church already is. The purpose clause removes any room for display: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines light as that ethereal agent or matter which makes objects perceptible to the sense of seeing, and figuratively instruction or knowledge; and conspicuous as open to the view, obvious to the eye, easy to be seen.
webster_full: LIGHT, n. That ethereal agent or matter which makes objects perceptible to the sense of seeing. Means of knowing; illumination of mind; instruction.
CONSPICUOUS, a. Open to the view; obvious to the eye; easy to be seen. Obvious to the mental eye; clearly or extensively known, perceived or understood.
CANDLESTICK, n. An instrument or utensil to hold a candle, made of different materials and in different forms.
HAMLET, n. A small village; a little cluster of houses in the country.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
scriptures: Mat 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Mat 5:15
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
Php 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world;
corruption_summary: A town named the village of the monks, and the city on a hill that cannot be hid.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is visibility cultivated for its own sake, which our Lord addresses two chapters later by forbidding alms done to be seen. The two passages are not in tension: the light is to be unhidden and the almsgiving is to be unadvertised, because the aim of the first is that men “glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16) and the aim of the second is that they should not glorify the giver. Everything turns on who receives the glory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church's conspicuousness is a given, not an achievement, and so is its obligation. “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick” (Mat 5:15) makes concealment the absurdity. Paul says the same of ordinary Christians in a bad city, that they “shine as lights in the world” (Php 2:15) among a crooked generation — and the shining is simply being what they are.
roots_summary: Irish Graig na Manach, village of the monks; Latin Vallis Sancti Salvatoris; Greek phos (G5457), light; Greek luchnia (G3087), a candlestick; Greek doxazo (G1392), to glorify.
roots_lines: Irish Graig na Manach — the village of the monks.
Latin Vallis Sancti Salvatoris — the valley of the holy Saviour.
Greek phos (G5457) — light; “Ye are the light of the world” (Mat 5:14).
Greek luchnia (G3087) — a lampstand, a candlestick; “but on a candlestick” (Mat 5:15).
Greek doxazo (G1392) — to glorify; “and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16).
usage: “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14) — a fact, not a goal.
“that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16) — seen works, unseen giver.
“shine as lights in the world” (Php 2:15) — said of ordinary believers.
